cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf group, including Mengku, Fengqing and Menghai large-leaf
processing: This is a plant group rather than a finished tea. Its leaf goes to pu-erh, made by sun-drying and pressing or piling, and to Dian Hong black tea, among others.
harvest_season: In pu-erh making, spring is the most valued picking and autumn is also respected; summer tea is less prized.
appearance_dry: As sun-dried maocha, typical of its use in pu-erh: long, thick, dark olive strips with visible pale tips.
appearance_liquor: Depends on the tea made from it: gold-orange in young raw pu-erh, red in Dian Hong.
appearance_wet: Large, thick, supple leaves, broader than those of small-leaf bushes.
taste_profile: As a raw material it makes strong, full-bodied tea, thanks to its high polyphenols and caffeine: bitter-sweet in young pu-erh, deep and red in black tea.

brewing.notes: A guide for young sun-dried leaf: it is strong, so keep steeps short. Finished teas from it have their own brewing notes.

vintage_note: Not sold under this name by the year; it reaches you as pu-erh, sold by year and region, or as Dian Hong, generally sold as a current-year black tea. On a label the words mainly say which plant was used, not grade or age.
description:
Dayezhong just means large-leaf variety, and in tea it points to Yunnan's tree-form plants from the Lancang River basin in the southwest and south of the province. It is the plant behind pu-erh and Dian Hong.

These are often true trees, with a natural height of five or six metres and some over twenty. The leaves are big and thick, and the group is known for high levels of polyphenols, caffeine and catechins compared with small-leaf bushes, although the figures vary from place to place.

That chemistry shows in the cup: more body and more bitterness, which sun-drying and age can turn into something long and sweet in pu-erh, and oxidation can turn into a deep red Dian Hong. Most drinkers meet it only through those teas.

Local selections have their own names, among them Mengku, Fengqing and Menghai large-leaf, Jingdong Daye and Jinggu Dabai. China's pu-erh standard requires this kind of leaf, so seeing it on a pack is normal rather than a special selling point.

To taste the plant's range, try a young raw pu-erh and a Dian Hong side by side.
history:
In November 1984 the Yunnan large-leaf variety was among the first 30 national-level tea cultivars approved in China. Its descendants have been planted across southern and southwestern China and the Jiangnan region.

Transplanting it was not always easy. In the 1950s the China Tea company pushed it into the middle and lower Yangtze to boost black tea, and nearly all these plantings failed, though one at Pingyang in Zhejiang took. Zhejiang breeders later used crosses with this plant to produce cultivars such as Zhenong 12 and Zhenong 21.

It is also the raw material of the Dian Hong tradition of Fengqing county, listed as national intangible heritage in 2014.
